vo.text: Jordan just got a job offer in Calgary. Same job. Same salary. One hundred thousand dollars.
Everybody says the same thing: move to Alberta, you'll pay less tax. And that's true. But is it enough?
Today we put Manitoba and Alberta in the ring. Taxes, the move itself, sales tax, and rent. Round by round, with real numbers.
Tax numbers are for twenty twenty-six, from the CRA's payroll tables and both provinces' rates. Rents come from the federal housing agency's latest survey.
Jordan is the same person from our last video. Thirty-four, single, working in IT, no other income.
Round one. Income tax. And the first surprise: most of Jordan's deductions don't change at all.
Federal tax is the same in both provinces: thirteen thousand, three hundred and two dollars.
CPP and EI are national programs too. Four thousand, six hundred and forty-six, and one thousand, one hundred and twenty-three. Identical.
Only one line moves. Provincial tax. In Manitoba, nine thousand, four hundred and eighty-four dollars.
In Alberta, six thousand, four hundred and seventy.
So Jordan keeps seventy-one thousand, four hundred and forty-five in Manitoba. And seventy-four thousand, four hundred and fifty-nine in Alberta.
That's three thousand and fourteen dollars a year. About two hundred and fifty-one dollars a month.
Why so big? Three reasons. Alberta's first rate is eight percent, on income up to sixty-one thousand, two hundred dollars. Manitoba starts at ten point eight.
Alberta's next rate is ten percent. Manitoba's is twelve point seven five.

And Alberta's basic personal amount, roughly the income you can earn before provincial tax kicks in, is twenty-two thousand, seven hundred and sixty-nine dollars. Manitoba's is fifteen thousand, seven hundred and eighty.
And the gap grows with income. At sixty thousand, Alberta saves about one thousand, nine hundred dollars. At a hundred and fifty thousand, about six thousand, six hundred and sixty-one.
Round one goes to Alberta. Clearly.
But there's a hidden round inside round one. Say Jordan's career goes well, and next year brings a ten thousand dollar raise.
Manitoba has a trap here. Its third rate, seventeen point four percent, starts at a hundred thousand dollars of taxable income. Jordan's raise lands right on top of it.
So in Manitoba, out of that ten thousand dollar raise, Jordan keeps six thousand, two hundred and sixty-two.
In Alberta, the next rate doesn't start until a hundred and fifty-four thousand, two hundred and fifty-nine. Jordan keeps six thousand, nine hundred and fifty.
Six hundred and eighty-eight dollars more, from the same raise. And the yearly gap grows to three thousand, seven hundred and two.
Round two. Timing. When should Jordan move?
Here's a rule a lot of people miss. For your tax return, your province is where you lived on December thirty-first.
So if Jordan moves in November, Alberta's rates apply to the provincial tax for the whole year. Even the months worked in Winnipeg.
For Jordan, that's the full three thousand and fourteen dollar difference for that year, just from moving before New Year's. All else equal.
The paycheques before the move still had Manitoba tax taken off. The difference gets settled when Jordan files.
Move on January second instead, and the whole year before is Manitoba's. Same move. Different calendar.
Round three. The move itself. Movers, a truck, a few nights in a hotel. It's not cheap.
But moving for a new job can be deductible. The rule: Jordan's new home has to be at least forty kilometres closer to the new work location. Winnipeg to Calgary clears that easily.
What counts? Movers, packing and storage. Travel, including meals and lodging on the way. Up to fifteen days of temporary living. Even the cost of breaking the old lease, and a new driver's licence.
Two catches. The deduction only comes off income earned at the new job. And if the employer paid for the move, Jordan can't claim the same costs twice.
Say Jordan spends five thousand dollars. At Jordan's rate in Alberta, that deduction is worth about one thousand, five hundred and twenty-five dollars. Keep every receipt.
Round four. Sales tax. Both provinces charge the five percent GST.
But Manitoba adds its own retail sales tax: seven percent on most goods and some services. Alberta has no provincial sales tax at all.
How much that saves depends on what Jordan buys. Not everything is taxed. So think of it this way: every thousand dollars of taxable shopping costs seventy dollars more in Manitoba.
A new laptop, furniture, appliances. It adds up. Round four, Alberta again.
Fifteen thousand dollars of taxable purchases in a year? That's one thousand and fifty dollars of Manitoba sales tax that Alberta doesn't charge.
Alberta is up three rounds to none. And this is where most videos stop. But Jordan still needs somewhere to live.
Round five. Rent. The federal housing agency surveys rents every October.
The average two-bedroom apartment in Winnipeg: one thousand, five hundred and seventy-one dollars a month.
In Calgary: one thousand, nine hundred and fourteen.
That's three hundred and forty-three dollars more every month. Four thousand, one hundred and sixteen a year.
Wait. That's bigger than the whole tax saving.

But Jordan is a new tenant, and new tenants pay whatever the market asks. For units that just turned over, the survey shows one thousand, five hundred and ninety-five in Winnipeg, and one thousand, eight hundred and thirty-six in Calgary.
That's a gap of two hundred and forty-one a month. Two thousand, eight hundred and ninety-two a year. Round five goes to Manitoba.
One honest note. These are city-wide averages for purpose-built apartments. Condos, houses, utilities, car insurance and the commute are not in this number. Price them for yourself.
So let's add it up. The tax saving: plus three thousand and fourteen.
Against the average rent gap, Jordan ends up one thousand, one hundred and two dollars behind.
Against new-tenant rents, Jordan is ahead by just one hundred and twenty-two dollars. That's basically a tie.
Then the sales tax can tip it. To win back eleven hundred and two dollars at seven percent, Jordan would need about fifteen thousand, seven hundred dollars a year of taxable purchases.
So, the verdict. Alberta's lower tax is real. Three thousand dollars a year at this salary. But on its own, it doesn't make the move a win.
The real decision is everything around the tax: the job, the rent you actually get quoted, and how you spend.
So before you move, run three numbers. Your provincial tax in both places. A real rent quote. And your yearly taxable shopping. Then time the move, and keep the receipts.
Next on this channel: eighty thousand, a hundred thousand, or a hundred and fifty thousand dollars. How much do you actually keep at each step? Subscribe, so you don't miss it.
